items.rationale: The model has no memory between calls; it sees only the text the program sends, which normally includes the earlier turns. Options c and d wrongly give the model its own storage; option a wrongly says nothing is carried over.
4 calls x 5,000 tokens = 20,000 input tokens, because the whole context is re-sent on every call. An answer of 5,000 treats the context as counted once.

The window is thrown away when the session ends, so the fact has to be saved outside it (a note or database) and read back next session. A bigger window does not outlive the session, the model keeps nothing on its own, and instructions are not training.

items.answer: Because retrieval only changes the text handed to the model on each call; the model reads the newly retrieved pages and has not learned the manual.
accepted: the model only reads what is retrieved
the new pages are retrieved and put in the context
retrieval hands the model the new text, it does not rely on training
the model never learned the manual, it reads the retrieved pages
items.rationale: Retrieval searches an index of the current text and appends the best chunks to the window. The model's knowledge is not changed, so only the index needs updating. A reply saying the model learned or was updated has the mechanism wrong.

items.answer: It costs input tokens on every call, and accuracy can drop as the window fills (context rot); retrieving only the right pages is cheaper and more accurate.
accepted: it is expensive because the whole pile is re-sent every call
context rot, the model recalls less well as the context grows
too many tokens per call, which costs more and lowers accuracy
fitting is not the same as working well
items.rationale: Either reason is fully correct: cost (the pile is re-sent and counted on every call) or accuracy (context rot). An answer that only says it will not fit treats the window size as the only limit.
